entities.name: Sima Ang
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sima Ang emerged as a prominent, albeit short-lived, figure during the tumultuous Chu–Han Contention (206–202 BCE), a critical interregnum in Chinese history following the collapse of the Qin Dynasty. As one of the Eighteen Kings established by Xiang Yu, the Hegemon-King of Western Chu, Sima Ang was designated King of Yin (殷王) in 206 BCE, ruling over a territory encompassing parts of modern-day Henan and Shanxi provinces. His rise epitomized the fragmentation of central authority and the intense competition among warlords seeking to carve out new domains from the ruins of the Qin Empire, positioning him as a minor but illustrative player in the broader struggle that would ultimately determine the shape of unified China.

Following the final defeat of the Qin at the Battle of Julu and the subsequent entry of Liu Bang into Guanzhong, Xiang Yu orchestrated the partition of the former Qin empire into eighteen kingdoms. Sima Ang, who had served as a general under Xiang Yu, was rewarded with the Kingdom of Yin, with his capital likely near modern-day Xiangyang (襄陽). His reign, however, was precarious and brief, caught between the ambitions of the two primary contenders, Xiang Yu and Liu Bang. His strategic position made him an early target for Liu Bang's forces as the latter began to consolidate power and challenge Xiang Yu's supremacy. Sima Ang's loyalty to Xiang Yu placed him squarely in the path of the emerging Han dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sima Ang's brief reign as King of Yin and his swift defeat by Han Xin represent a minor but illustrative episode in the larger Chu–Han Contention, demonstrating the initial fragmentation and subsequent consolidation that led to the unified Han Dynasty.
